messages.author: ca9707e227b6d438
messages.subject: blavFitIndices vs fit.measures
parts:
Hi,

I am looking at model fit for a bSEM model, and wondering which set of fit statistics is most appropriate, and how they differ? 

In my model PPP = .000, which indicates poor fit, but the blavfitindicies indicate good fit (BRMSEA = 0.035, BGammaHat = .964).

Does anyone have any advice on which to use or how to explain these differences? 


Thanks, Dan.

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: blavFitIndices vs fit.measures
parts:
Dan,

The brmsea/bgammahat stuff is very new; I'm not sure that we fully
understand their behaviors yet. However, the ppp is related to the X2
statistic in ML estimation, and brmsea is obviously related to rmsea
in ML estimation. In the ML case, people often discuss the fact that
X2 tells you your model is bad more often than RMSEA, so I would guess
that a similar thing is going on here.

Ed

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: blavFitIndices vs fit.measures
parts:
Dan

I developed these posterior distributions for similar relative fit indices in BSEM. Hopefully the paper will be publish soon.

As Ed mentioned, the ppp has the limitation that it behaves very similar to the p-value of the chi square test in ML SEM. This means that is sensitive to sample size, model type. For these reasons the relative fit indices were developed in ML.

From our tests, with uninformative priors, the mean of the posterior distribution of these fit indices are equivalent to the estimate from ML SEM. In ML SEM the most common practice is to use cutoff to said that the model presents god or bad fit, we do not recommend this (in either ML or Bayesian) since each fit index is sensitive to different characteristics (there is no perfect fit index). So, we recommend to use the posterior distribution of the relative fit indices (mean, SD, CI), using these are diagnostic tools for strengths and weakness of the model, instead of the binary decision of fit/dont fit.

An advantage of these posterior distributions of fit indices over the ML estimates is that with the posterior distribution we can account for uncertainty, helping to use for for a continuous inference.

Also, as Ed mentioned, these are new and just developed, so we still need to test them further to understand better its behavior.

Hope this helps

messages.subject: Re: blavFitIndices vs fit.measures
parts:
It could be that a reviewer mentioned that, but the bad behavior of the PPP is well known. You can easily add a couple of references to why it is not trusted, and you are judging the fit in function of the relative fit measures. Hopefully our paper soon, there is also the Levy paper and Hoofs

Levy, R. (2011). Bayesian Data-Model Fit Assessment for Structural Equation Modeling. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 18(4), 663–685. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2011.607723
Hoofs, H., van de Schoot, R., Jansen, N. W. H., & Kant, Ij. (2017). Evaluating model fit in Bayesian confirmatory factor analysis with large samples: Simulation study introducing the BRMSEA. Educational and Psychological Measurement. https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164417709314

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: blavFitIndices vs fit.measures
parts:
Hi

About an example, please look at the help page of the blavFitIndices function. There are examples, like:

 ## Not run:
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
## fit target model
fit1 <- bcfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, cp = "fa",
             n.chains = 2, burnin = 1000, sample = 1000)

## fit null model to calculate CFI, TLI, and NFI
null.model <- c(paste0("x", 1:9, " ~~ x", 1:9), paste0("x", 1:9, " ~ 1"))
fit0 <- bcfa(null.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, cp = "fa",
             n.chains = 2, burnin = 1000, sample = 1000)

## calculate posterior distributions of fit indices

## The default method mimics fit indices derived from ML estimation
ML <- blavFitIndices(fit1, baseline.model = fit0)
ML
summary(ML)

> summary(ML)

Posterior summary statistics and highest posterior density (HPD) 90% credible intervals for devm-based fit indices:

               EAP Median   MAP    SD lower upper
BRMSEA       0.097  0.097 0.095 0.006 0.088 0.107
BGammaHat    0.956  0.957 0.958 0.005 0.949 0.965
adjBGammaHat 0.891  0.892 0.896 0.013 0.872 0.913
BMc          0.903  0.903 0.907 0.011 0.886 0.922
BCFI         0.930  0.931 0.933 0.009 0.917 0.945
BTLI         0.887  0.888 0.893 0.014 0.867 0.911
BNFI         0.909  0.910 0.912 0.008 0.898 0.924

####
The summary of the blavFitIndices object will provide 3 central tendency measures (mean/EAP, median, and mode/MAP). The most recommended one is the mean or median. ALso provides the standard deviation, and Credible interval for each fit index. The fit indices are in the same metric as the maximum likelihood ones. So, for example for CFI value closer to 1 is better.
Now, we know that the strict cutoff method of interpretation (for example that CFI has to be higher than 0.9) is not appropriate for every model. So, using these strict cutoffs is not recommended. This leaves a problem, because there is no GENERALIZABLE recommended way to interpret these overall fit measures.

We recommend to use them as general guidelines, as you would look for patterns of good of bad fit the different indices. There are not develop (these of the maximum likelihood ones) to do a hypothesis testing to choose a model. Fit indices should be look more like effect sizes misfit.

With the SD and Credible intervals you can look at how variable the indices are, this would lead for you to make a decision on how much uncertainty is related to sampling variability. For example, if you have a "good" CFI mean 0.93, but the credible interval is very wide, like 0.7 to 0.99. This would indicate that in general shows a central tendency close to high values of CFI, but there is low confidence for this value, as could range drastically based on your data.

For these Bayesian Fit indices, our paper is still under review, I hope it will be done and ready to share soon. For review you could look and general literature on model evaluation Bentler & Bonett (1980), MacCallum et al. (1996), (Beauducel & Wittmann, 2005; Fan & Sivo, 2005; Heene, Hilbert, Draxler, Ziegler, & Bühner, 2011; Heene, Hilbert, Freudenthaler, & Bühner, 2012), Marsh, Hau, & Wen, 2004), Jorgensen et al., 2017

Sorry, I dont access to the full reference for each right now

Hope this helps

messages.subject: Re: blavFitIndices vs fit.measures
parts:
Yes, you have to write the lavaan model syntax for the null model, then estimate it with blavaan and give that blavaan object in the function

In the example in the help page it estimates the null model as fito, and then adds it int the baseline.model argument of the blavFitIndices function

## Not run:
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
## fit target model
fit1 <- bcfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, cp = "fa",
             n.chains = 2, burnin = 1000, sample = 1000)

## fit null model to calculate CFI, TLI, and NFI
null.model <- c(paste0("x", 1:9, " ~~ x", 1:9), paste0("x", 1:9, " ~ 1"))
fit0 <- bcfa(null.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, cp = "fa",
             n.chains = 2, burnin = 1000, sample = 1000)

## calculate posterior distributions of fit indices

## The default method mimics fit indices derived from ML estimation
ML <- blavFitIndices(fit1, baseline.model = fit0)
ML
summary(ML)

The summary of the blavFitIndices object will provide 3 central tendency measures (mean/EAP, median, and mode/MAP). The most recommended one is the mean or median. ALso provides the standard deviation, and Credible interval for each fit index. The fit indices are in the same metric as the maximum likelihood ones. So, for example for CFI value closer to 1 is better.
Now, we know that the strict cutoff method of interpretation (for example that CFI has to be higher than 0.9) is not appropriate for every model. So, using these strict cutoffs is not recommended. This leaves a problem, because there is no GENERALIZABLE recommended way to interpret these overall fit measures.

We recommend to use them as general guidelines, as you would look for patterns of good of bad fit the different indices. There are not develop (these of the maximum likelihood ones) to do a hypothesis testing to choose a model. Fit indices should be look more like effect sizes misfit.

With the SD and Credible intervals you can look at how variable the indices are, this would lead for you to make a decision on how much uncertainty is related to sampling variability. For example, if you have a "good" CFI mean 0.93, but the credible interval is very wide, like 0.7 to 0.99. This would indicate that in general shows a central tendency close to high values of CFI, but there is low confidence for this value, as could range drastically based on your data.

For these Bayesian Fit indices, our paper is still under review, I hope it will be done and ready to share soon. For review you could look and general literature on model evaluation Bentler & Bonett (1980), MacCallum et al. (1996), (Beauducel & Wittmann, 2005; Fan & Sivo, 2005; Heene, Hilbert, Draxler, Ziegler, & Bühner, 2011; Heene, Hilbert, Freudenthaler, & Bühner, 2012), Marsh, Hau, & Wen, 2004), Jorgensen et al., 2017

Sorry, I dont access to the full reference for each right now

Hope this helps

segunda-feira, 3 de Dezembro de 2018 às 19:36:57 UTC, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal escreveu:
Dan

I developed these posterior distributions for similar relative fit indices in BSEM. Hopefully the paper will be publish soon.

As Ed mentioned, the ppp has the limitation that it behaves very similar to the p-value of the chi square test in ML SEM. This means that is sensitive to sample size, model type. For these reasons the relative fit indices were developed in ML.

From our tests, with uninformative priors, the mean of the posterior distribution of these fit indices are equivalent to the estimate from ML SEM. In ML SEM the most common practice is to use cutoff to said that the model presents god or bad fit, we do not recommend this (in either ML or Bayesian) since each fit index is sensitive to different characteristics (there is no perfect fit index). So, we recommend to use the posterior distribution of the relative fit indices (mean, SD, CI), using these are diagnostic tools for strengths and weakness of the model, instead of the binary decision of fit/dont fit.

An advantage of these posterior distributions of fit indices over the ML estimates is that with the posterior distribution we can account for uncertainty, helping to use for for a continuous inference.

Also, as Ed mentioned, these are new and just developed, so we still need to test them further to understand better its behavior.

Hope this helps

messages.subject: Re: blavFitIndices vs fit.measures
parts:
That is part of the issue on BSEM, what a null model should be becomes a wider question.

If you want to use the default SEM standard of null model, the independence model, you can estimate the CFA with lavaan and extract the null model from it. For example:

library(lavaan)

## The famous Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)

partable_null <- lav_partable_independence(fit)

Then you give partable_null, as the model to blavaan. This is the parameter table from lavaan for the respective null model
